referred_to_by.content: A visual anchor for the project: art, price, reform, and institutional display held together as one unstable field.

The work exists as an object, and the image published here is a photograph of it. The studio states, on 2026-09-22, that Art Market Reform exists and is held in its own collection, and that the file published with this record is a photograph of that physical work rather than a born-digital image. That is the studio's statement about its own holdings, recorded as such; nobody outside the studio has examined the object, and no measurement, medium, support or date of making is recorded here because none has been supplied. Two consequences should be read off it. The first is that this record's modelling is provisional and known to be incomplete: it types the work as a digital object classified as a digital image, which describes the photograph and not the thing photographed, and a fuller record would describe the object and treat this file as documentation of it. That correction is deferred until the object's particulars are to hand, and is noted here so that a reader does not take the present typing for a considered claim about what the work is. The second is that the photograph's own date is not established: the file as published carries no camera metadata, having been re-encoded, so it dates neither the object nor the photographing.

A second painting carries this title, and it is the one the studio put on its website. The Internet Archive's capture of the studio's site on 2014-12-18, and again on 2016-01-11, carries a photograph of a painting lettered 'ART MARKET REFORM' across a blue ground worked with white. That is not the painting photographed for this record, which sets the words over a dense multicoloured ground with 'Art' in block letters and 'Market Reform' in script. Two paintings therefore share the title, and the one a third party dates is not the one published here. The consequence for this record is that its subject is ambiguous as it stands: it names a title, publishes a photograph of one object, and does not say which object the title's other uses in this collection refer to. A fuller record should describe a set and say which painting each statement is about.

Named, and called a title, in a letter to a museum on 2013-09-12. The studio's letter to the Jordan Schnitzer Museum of Art introduces two works by name: 'Two popular examples of Metaconceptual Art, which are ongoing through time and space as well, are titled "Art Market Reform" , and "Art Tax"'. It then glosses this one: 'Promoting Art Tax on the local, state, national, and international levels to encourage and promote accountability, transparency, and regulation in the Art Market and Art World.' That is the earliest dated naming of this work held in this collection, it is in the artist's own words, and it was delivered to a named institution which produced its own copy from its archive in 2026, so the date does not rest on the studio's mailbox alone. Three limits go with it. The letter attests that the title was in use on that date; it does not date the making of the image published with this record, and its own phrase, that the works are 'ongoing through time and space', describes them as continuing rather than finished. The letter attaches images but names none of them, so nothing in it identifies the file published here as the thing it names. And a title used in 2013 says nothing about 2009 or before.
